title: Envy at work
hook: a colleague's success, and the price they paid for it

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ambition: James and John asked for the best seats, and Jesus turned greatness into service. Your line was what is it for.

The announcement goes out. Someone else got the role, the bonus, the project everyone wanted. The congratulations in the chat arrive fast, a row of little hands clapping. Underneath, for some people, something slower starts to chew. The book of Proverbs, in the King James Bible, has a line for it: "A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones." It doesn't make a sound. It just sits in the bones. Today: muditā.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE GOT IT.` → `ENVY THE ROTTENNESS OF THE BONES.` → `ENVY AT WORK.`

segments.voice: First, an old voice that found envy inside work itself. Ecclesiastes says, "Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour." Notice the word right: good work, done well, and the neighbor envies it. Envy isn't a sign that something went wrong at the office. It follows good work around. Second, the price. Envy looks at a colleague's win and skips the bill. The promotion may have come with late nights, a move, a missed dinner, a risk that could have gone the other way. Or it may not have. Often we simply don't know: envy works from half a picture. An honest question helps. Would I take the whole trade, price included? If yes, that tells us what we want. If no, the envy loosens. Third, a practice from Buddhism with a name: muditā. Buddhist teaching names it as one of four qualities to cultivate, along with loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity, and it means gladness at someone else's good fortune. In the meditation manuals it isn't left to arrive on its own. It's practiced on purpose, bringing to mind a person who is doing well and wishing that their good fortune last. Fourth, Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Rejoicing comes first in the line. Envy says their win is my loss. These voices say their win is theirs, and a share of the gladness is free to anyone who wants it.
screen: `EVERY RIGHT WORK IS ENVIED.` · `ENVY SKIPS THE BILL.` · `MUDITĀ: GLAD FOR THEM.` · `REJOICE WITH THEM THAT REJOICE.` · then, large: `THEIR WIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a colleague or a friend whose success has stung a little, and notice where the sting sits without pushing it away. Allow that their win had a price, the parts nobody posts, even if you don't know what it was. Then, the way muditā is practiced, wish them well, may this good thing stay with them, or if you pray, hold them in your own tradition's words.
Muditā. Gladness at someone else's good fortune, a quality Buddhist teaching asks us to practice on purpose. Today's word.
Your line: their win. Muditā is the practice of being glad for it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate muditā, gladness at others' good fortune, as one of the four brahmaviharas, often in meditation; Christians read Romans 12:15 as a call to share in others' joy and grief.

notes: Muditā as one of the four brahmaviharas (with mettā, karuṇā, upekkhā) and the meditation of wishing a prosperous person's good fortune to last are paraphrased from Visuddhimagga IX; a Buddhist Keeper should confirm the description and the Devanagari/pronunciation in the original game.
The 'price' section is the index hook, framed as a question, with no claims about what success costs.
